name: Proposed projects on the Projects page

pr.title: Show projects proposed in open pull requests on the Projects page
pr.head: 6a3a95d03d4a4aa742004ba210cecdf940f7122b

summary: The Projector site's Projects page lists the plans under docs/projects, built from the checkout of the default branch. A new plan reaches that branch only when its pull request merges, and Projector writes plans as pull requests so that people review them first. So the page leaves out exactly the plans that need a reader's attention.

The site already holds those plans. The review loop publishes a summary of every pull request to the hidden ref refs/projector/summaries, and each summary stores the pull request's diff as diff.patch. A new file's diff holds every line of the file. This pull request reads those diffs at build time and lists each plan an open pull request adds as a proposed project, with a Proposed #N badge that links its review.

1. Ask GitHub first. The build now asks for each pull request's status before it links any summary. It is the same one query per pull request as before, moved earlier, and it now also returns whether the branch is in a fork.
  2. Pick the plans. From the newest summary of each open, same-repository pull request, it takes every new <projects dir>/<name>/readme.md the checkout does not have, rebuilds its text from the diff, and loads it with the parser project list uses.
  3. Serve them like any project. Each proposed project is an ordinary entry in site.json with an extra proposed field, served at projects/<name>/, the address it keeps after the merge, together with the other Markdown files its diff adds.
  4. Mark them on the page. The badge appears on the Projects page, in the sidebar, and in search results. A banner tops every page of the project and names the pull request, its review status, and the head the site shows.

This is the top of a two-layer stack. The layer beneath, #225, deploys the site when a pull request closes, so a proposal leaves the page as soon as its pull request merges or closes. The plan stays in-progress until a throwaway plan's pull request is opened and closed against the deployed site.

cards.title: Terms used on this page
cards.html:
• Proposed project: a project whose readme.md is a new file in the newest summary's diff of an open pull request from this repository, and that the checkout does not have.
  • Checkout: the tree the site is built from, the default branch on a deploy.
  • Summary: the guided review page the review loop publishes per pull request head, stored with its diff.patch under summaries/<number>/<head>/.
  • pr_status: the one GraphQL query per pull request that returns its state, base branch, reviews, and now fork.
  • also: the other open pull requests that propose a plan of the same name.

cards.title: When a pull request proposes a plan
cards.html:
CaseResult
Open, branch in this repositoryProposed
Merged or closedNot proposed
Branch in a forkNot proposed; its review stays
Status unknown (GitHub not reachable)Not proposed; one warning with the count
Checkout has the name or the pathCheckout wins
Plan fails to loadSkipped with a warning; takes no name
Two pull requests propose one nameLowest number wins; others in also

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html: The Projector review of head 6a3a95d found one P2: a repository whose projects directory sits inside a hidden folder, such as .plans, now fails the whole site build, because the search index reads plans from content/ and those plans are never copied there. It is flagged on the search index line below. One suggestion: by_pr's type annotation still names a two-item tuple.

groups.title: Reading a plan out of a diff
groups.kicker: Two small helpers let the build load a plan from text rather than from a file, and the status query learns about forks.
intro: A proposed plan exists only as lines in a stored diff, never as a file on disk. To treat it exactly like a checkout plan, the build needs the plan's text and a parser that accepts text. Using the same parser means a plan shows as proposed exactly when project list would load it after the merge.

• project_from_text, in core.py, is the half of ProjectStore._project_from_path that runs after the file is read: the name check and the status, priority, and owner checks. _project_from_path now reads the file and calls it.
  • new_file_text, in summary.py, joins a new file's added lines from parse_diff's hunks and keeps or drops the final newline as the diff's \ No newline at end of file marker says.
  • pr_status asks GitHub for isCrossRepository in the same query and returns it as fork.

checks.text: parse_diff splits the patch on \n alone, so a plan with CRLF line endings keeps its \r bytes and the rebuilt text matches the file. Checked by reading parse_diff; the build test compares the content byte for byte.
fork is True only when GitHub says so. The build treats anything but an explicit False as a fork, so a status without the field proposes nothing.

files.note: Moves the plan checks into project_from_text unchanged, so the build and project list share one parser.

checks.text: The body is the old _project_from_path code with relative renamed name. Error messages still name the plan by its repository path.

groups.title: Finding proposed projects in the site build
groups.kicker: The build asks for statuses first, picks the proposed plans, writes their files, and links summaries over both lists.
intro: build_summaries reads every summary and keeps each pull request's versions, newest first. Before this change it linked each summary to the checkout's projects while reading it, and asked GitHub for the pull request's status afterwards. Now it reads everything, asks for every status, and only then links, because a summary can link to a project that another pull request proposes.

The new proposed_projects function does the selection the overview's table describes. It writes each proposed plan and its Markdown files under content/, never over a checkout file. HTML pages, images, and data files are left out on purpose: the site shows an HTML page unsandboxed on its own origin, and a proposal has not been merged.

build_site then merges the proposed projects into its project list before it assigns routes, so routes, site.json, search.json, and each project's list of reviews include them. search_index now reads every document from the site's content/ copy, so proposed pages are indexed the same way as checkout pages.

checks.text: The build still asks pr_status once per pull request. Every ProposedProjectTests build asserts the call count, and the suite ran 572 tests OK at this head.

files.note: Adds proposed_projects, reorders build_summaries so statuses come before linking, and makes search_index read from content/.

checks.text: Every status is asked here, before linking. The loop below reuses asked[number] instead of asking again.
Only an explicitly open pull request whose fork is False proposes. An unknown status was counted just above and leads to one warning line.
The checkout wins twice: on a project name it loads, and on any file at the same path, even a plan that failed to load in the checkout.
Pull requests are visited lowest number first, so the first plan that loads takes the name and later ones join its also list. A plan that fails to load never gets here.
Hidden folders are judged relative to the repository root, as pages_under does for checkout files.

This line now reads each plan from its copy under content/. A checkout whose projects.dir is inside a hidden folder, such as .plans, has its plans loaded but never copied, because pages_under skips dot-folders. project site build then exits 65 with a missing-file error and the whole deploy fails, where the base built it. The open review finding asks search_index to skip a document that has no copy under content/.

files.note: Returns the configured projects directory even when the checkout lacks it, so a repository's first plan can be proposed, and counts proposed projects in the build's summary line.

checks.text: Before, a checkout with no projects directory passed None, and the build could not tell where a proposed plan would live.

groups.title: Showing proposed projects on the page
groups.kicker: One constant labels the badge and the banner, and GitHub links on a proposed page point at the proposal's head.
intro: The site's front end is TypeScript in site/src/, compiled to site/assets/site.js, which is committed. It reads site.json, which now gives a proposed project a proposed object: the pull request's number, the summary's head, and also.

• Projects page. A proposed project sits in its status group with a Proposed #N badge that links its review. The note under the heading counts proposed projects, and typing proposed in the filter keeps them.
  • Project pages. Every page of a proposed project opens with a banner: the pull request, its title and review status as the Reviews index draws them, the head shown, and any other proposals of the name.
  • GitHub links. View on GitHub and Markdown links to repository files the site lacks point at the proposal's head, where the file exists, rather than at the site's branch.
  • Sidebar and search. Both draw the badge.

checks.text: Rendered a built fixture site in headless Chromium at 1100 and 375 pixels: the badge sits in the right status group, the banner names the other proposal, a checkout project's sidebar badges its proposed nested project, and a pull request title holding markup shows as text.
npm run check reported nothing, and npm run build left site/assets/site.js unchanged.

files.note: Adds the Proposal type, and proposed on a project and on a search entry.
Adds PROPOSED, proposedBadge, and proposalBanner, and threads a ref through repoUrl, renderMarkdown, and showPage.

checks.text: ref is the proposal's head on any page of a proposed project, and the site's branch everywhere else. A checkout project nested under a proposed one keeps the site's branch.
The title and status come from the pull request's row in site.json's reviews, which every proposed project has, since its summary is what proposed it.

files.note: Styles the badge and banner with the existing --info colours, which already have light and dark values.

groups.title: Tests
groups.kicker: Build tests for each selection rule, node tests for the page, and unit tests for the helpers.
intro: ProposedProjectTests publishes fake summaries into a temporary checkout and replaces pr_status with a fake, one case per row of the plan's acceptance table. ProposedViewTests runs functions from the compiled site.js under node. The unit tests cover new_file_text, the fork field, and project_from_text against ProjectStore.

groups.title: Documentation and the plan
groups.kicker: The CLI and site docs describe proposed projects, and the plan records what implementation settled.
intro: docs/cli.md explains when a pull request proposes a project and what the build prints. docs/site.md mentions the badge in its menu description. The plan gains section 8, which records how the work splits across #225 and this pull request, the details implementation settled, the measured build time before and after, and the one acceptance check left for after the merge.

checks.text: The plan stays in-progress because its last acceptance check, opening and closing a throwaway plan's pull request against the deployed site, can only run after this merges.
